title: Cycle Detection: Course Schedule
oneLiner: Can every course be finished? Only if the prerequisite graph has no cycle, and a DFS that remembers which nodes are on its current path finds one.
keyTakeaway: Give every node one of three colours: unvisited, on the current DFS path, or done. While exploring a node, reaching a neighbour that is ON THE PATH means you have walked in a circle: a cycle. Reaching a DONE neighbour is fine, because everything after it was already checked. A plain visited set can't tell those two cases apart, which is why it needs the third colour.
explanation:
There are numCourses courses, numbered 0 to numCourses - 1. Each pair [a, b] in prerequisites means you must take course b before course a. Return true if it is possible to finish every course, false otherwise.

Draw each pair as a directed edge b -> a ("b unlocks a"). If following edges ever brings you back to where you started, those courses each wait on another one in the loop, so none of them can be taken first. If there is no such loop, the graph is a DAG (directed acyclic graph) and some order always works. So the question is just: does this directed graph contain a cycle?

Depth-first search answers it if you track three states per node. Unvisited (white) nodes haven't been reached yet. A node turns gray when DFS enters it, meaning it is on the path from the current starting point down to where the search is now. It turns black (done) when every edge out of it has been fully explored. Run DFS from every node that is still white. Inside DFS(u): mark u gray, then for each edge u -> v, if v is gray you have found a cycle (v is an ancestor of u on the current path, and the edge goes back up to it); if v is white, recurse into it; if v is black, skip it. After the loop, mark u black.

Why not one visited set? Take the diamond 0 -> 1, 0 -> 2, 1 -> 3, 2 -> 3. DFS goes 0, 1, 3, finishes, backs out to 0, then goes to 2 and sees 3 again. 3 was visited, but it is not on the current path (0, 2), so this is not a loop: two routes merging into the same course is perfectly fine. Only the gray/black split tells "I'm standing on a node I came through" apart from "I already finished that node earlier".

Each node is entered once and each edge followed once, so the cost is O(V + E) time, with O(V + E) space for the adjacency list plus the colour array and the recursion stack. A long chain of prerequisites makes the recursion as deep as the chain; for very large inputs use an explicit stack, or use Kahn's in-degree algorithm instead (see the topological sort lesson), which answers the same question by checking whether every course gets processed.

The visualization runs DFS on edges 0 -> 1, 0 -> 2, 1 -> 3, 2 -> 3, 2 -> 4, 4 -> 5, 5 -> 2. Lines are drawn without arrowheads, so the message says which way each edge points. Dashed amber nodes are gray (on the path) and green nodes are done.

visualizationSteps.message: Edges point from a prerequisite to the course it unlocks: 0 -> 1, 0 -> 2, 1 -> 3, 2 -> 3, 2 -> 4, 4 -> 5, 5 -> 2. Every course starts unvisited. Start DFS from course 0.
Enter 0 and mark it as on the path. Current path: 0.
Enter 1 and mark it as on the path. Current path: 0 -> 1.
Enter 3 and mark it as on the path. Current path: 0 -> 1 -> 3.
3 has no outgoing edges. Mark it done and step back.
Every edge out of 1 is explored without finding a loop. Mark it done and step back to 0.
Enter 2 and mark it as on the path. Current path: 0 -> 2.
Edge 2 -> 3, but 3 is already done. It was reached by another route and fully checked, so this is not a loop. Skip it.
Enter 4 and mark it as on the path. Current path: 0 -> 2 -> 4.
Enter 5 and mark it as on the path. Current path: 0 -> 2 -> 4 -> 5.
Edge 5 -> 2, and 2 is ON the current path (0 -> 2 -> 4 -> 5). Following edges led back to 2: that is a cycle, so return false.

The cycle 2 -> 4 -> 5 -> 2 means courses 2, 4 and 5 each wait on another one of them, so not every course can be finished. Remove the edge 5 -> 2 and the same search would mark everything done and return true.

recognitionSignals: Tasks, courses, or build steps with prerequisites, and the question is only WHETHER they can all be done, not in which order.
"Is there a circular dependency?", "can this deadlock?", or "does this directed graph have a cycle?" in any disguise.
The edges are one-way. (For an undirected graph, cycle detection is simpler: any visited neighbour other than the parent you came from closes a loop.)
gotchas: A single visited set reports false cycles on diamond shapes, where two paths reach the same node. You need separate "on the current path" and "done" states.
Mark the node done (black) AFTER exploring all its edges, not when you enter it; marking it early hides real cycles that pass through it.
Start a DFS from every still-unvisited node, not just from node 0. The cycle can be in a part of the graph that 0 can't reach.
A pair [a, a] is a course that requires itself: a cycle of length 1. The gray check catches it as long as you mark the node gray before looking at its edges.
confusableWith: Topological Sort: Order Tasks by Dependency (this track) works on the same prerequisite graph but has to RETURN an order, which Kahn's in-degree algorithm produces directly. Kahn's also answers this lesson's question (a cycle exists exactly when some course never reaches in-degree 0), so either approach is fine here.

Union-Find: Count Connected Components (this track) detects cycles in UNDIRECTED graphs (an edge joining two nodes already in the same set). It doesn't work for directed edges: a -> b and c -> b share a set but form no cycle.

complexity.note: Each course is entered once and each prerequisite edge followed once. Space is the adjacency list (V + E) plus the colour array and a recursion stack up to V deep.
